title: The Town Clock Debate
passage:
In the center of Aki's town stood a clock tower built almost eighty years ago. The clock had once been an important public service, but nearly everyone now carried a phone. When the town announced that the mechanism needed an expensive repair, some residents questioned whether the clock was still worth maintaining. The debate seemed simple at first: either spend public money on an old object or use the money for something more useful. Aki's civics class decided to study the issue. They began by asking residents what the tower meant to them. Older people often described it as a landmark connected with memories of festivals and school trips. Shop owners said visitors used it as an easy meeting point. Younger residents were less attached to the clock itself but liked the open square around it. A few people argued strongly against repair, pointing out that the town also needed money for road maintenance and child-care services. The students then examined the repair estimate. They learned that there were several options rather than one fixed cost. Replacing the entire mechanism would be expensive but reliable. Repairing only the damaged parts would cost less now but might require another repair later. A third option was to stop the clock while preserving the tower as a monument. Each choice changed both cost and function. The class invited a local historian and an engineer to speak. The historian warned that once working parts were removed, restoring the original function in the future could become difficult. The engineer explained that old equipment sometimes required custom parts, which increased cost, but also noted that regular maintenance could extend its life. Neither expert told the students what the town should do. Instead, they described consequences that were easy to miss. Aki's group proposed a public survey, but their teacher asked how the survey would be designed. If the question simply asked, Should we repair the clock, people might answer differently depending on whether they knew the price or the alternatives. The students created a longer form showing three options with estimated costs and likely future maintenance. The results did not produce an overwhelming winner. The lowest-cost repair received the most support, but many comments asked the town to seek private donations rather than paying entirely from taxes. Eventually, the town chose that approach. It funded basic safety work, while a local association raised money for the clock mechanism. The solution did not remove all criticism. Some residents believed public heritage should be fully supported by taxes, while others thought no public money should be used at all. Aki learned that disagreement does not always disappear after more information is provided. People can understand the same facts and still value goals differently. Yet better information can improve the quality of disagreement by making trade-offs visible. The clock now works again, but for Aki the more important lesson was how public choices are shaped not only by facts, but also by the way questions are framed and by what communities decide is worth preserving.

The class later compared its survey with a second survey that asked only a yes-or-no question about repair. The simple survey produced stronger opinions, while the detailed survey produced more comments about conditions and funding. Aki realized that asking people to choose after showing costs and alternatives did not merely collect an existing opinion; it sometimes changed or refined that opinion. Several residents who first supported full repair moved toward partial repair when they saw the maintenance estimate, while others became more supportive after learning how much local businesses used the square. The students concluded that public consultation should not be treated as a machine for measuring fixed preferences. It can also be a process in which people learn, compare values, and reconsider priorities while considering costs, alternatives, and consequences. It also showed them that survey design can shape the conversation itself.
translation:
秋の町の中心には、約八十年前に建てられた時計塔がありました。かつては重要な公共設備でしたが、今ではほとんどの人がスマートフォンを持っています。高額な修理が必要だと分かると、『古い物に税金を使うより他の用途に回すべきだ』という意見が出ました。秋の公民の授業ではこの問題を調べることになりました。住民に聞くと、高齢者は祭りや学校行事の記憶と結びついた象徴として語り、商店主は待ち合わせ場所として役立つと言いました。若者は時計そのものへの思い入れは弱くても、周囲の広場を好んでいました。一方、道路整備や子育て支援を優先すべきだという反対意見もありました。さらに修理費を調べると、全交換、部分修理、時計を止めて塔だけ保存するという複数の案があり、費用と機能がそれぞれ異なりました。歴史家は、動く機能を失うと将来の復元が難しくなる可能性を指摘し、技術者は古い機械は特注部品で高くなる一方、定期整備で寿命を延ばせると説明しました。生徒たちは住民アンケートを提案しましたが、先生は質問の作り方が答えを左右すると指摘します。単に『修理すべきか』と聞くのではなく、三つの案、費用、将来の維持費を示して調査しました。結果は圧倒的ではなく、低コストの部分修理が最も多かったものの、税金だけでなく寄付を募る案も多く寄せられました。最終的に町は安全面の基本工事を公費で行い、機械部分は地域団体が寄付を集めました。それでも、文化財は税金で守るべきだという人も、税金を一切使うべきでないという人も残りました。秋は、情報が増えれば必ず意見が一致するわけではないと学びます。同じ事実を理解しても、何を大切にするかは異なるからです。ただし、選択の代償を見える形にすれば、議論の質は高められます。時計は再び動き始めましたが、秋にとって本当の学びは、公共の選択が事実だけでなく、問いの立て方や地域が何を残す価値があると考えるかによって形づくられることでした。

クラスは、修理の賛否だけを尋ねる単純なアンケートとも結果を比べました。単純な質問では強い賛否が出やすい一方、費用や選択肢を示した詳しい調査では条件や資金についての意見が多くなりました。秋は、アンケートは固定した意見を測るだけではなく、情報を得ることで人の考えが変わったり具体化したりする場合があると気づきました。最初は全面修理を支持した人が維持費を見て部分修理へ変わる一方、商店が広場をよく利用していると知って修理への支持を強める人もいました。住民参加は単なる意見の集計ではなく、費用や選択肢、結果を考えながら価値を比較し、優先順位を見直す過程にもなります。また、質問の作り方そのものが議論の形を変えることも学びました。
